nodes.label: Zoonoses from herds
nodes.place: Near East and Eurasian farming villages
nodes.desc: Living with cattle, sheep, pigs and fowl passed animal diseases to people: measles from rinderpest, influenza from birds via pigs and poultry, brucellosis and anthrax as herders' and tanners' diseases. It needed domestic herds kept beside houses; it made farming villages sicker than forager bands.

nodes.label: Crowd diseases
nodes.desc: Measles, smallpox and other immunising diseases persist only where a population of a few hundred thousand supplies new children each year (unchecked). Measles split from rinderpest around 528 BCE (range 1174 BCE to 165 CE) by a molecular clock (checked). Towns became reservoirs and the urban sink began.

nodes.label: Black Death wage shock
nodes.desc: Plague killed a third to a half of Europe in 1347 to 1352 and recurred for three centuries. English real farm wages rose by about two thirds despite the labour statutes (parts 05, 06); land went to sheep, labourers ate and dressed better, and sumptuary law followed.

nodes.label: Columbian die-off
nodes.desc: Smallpox, measles, influenza, then malaria and yellow fever killed about 56 million in the Americas by 1600, roughly 90% (contested in detail, part 11). Land without labour made the mita, the encomienda and the Atlantic slave trade's plantations.

nodes.label: Malaria limits settlement
nodes.place: Marshes of Europe; West Africa; the Caribbean
nodes.desc: Malaria and yellow fever made marshes, coasts and the tropics deadly to newcomers: in West Africa often half of new European arrivals died in their first year (unchecked). Europeans traded from forts rather than settled, and planters bought enslaved Africans with partial immunity (contested).

nodes.label: Marsh and fen drainage
nodes.place: English Fens; Roman Campagna; Pontine Marshes
nodes.desc: Draining marshes made land, waterways and health at once: the Fens from the 17th century, the Pontine Marshes in the 1930s. Burial rates in marsh parishes had run far above upland ones (Dobson, unchecked).

nodes.label: Cinchona bark and quinine
nodes.desc: Andean cinchona bark was taken up by Jesuits as a fever cure in the 1630s; Pelletier and Caventou isolated quinine in 1820 (checked). Prophylaxis from the 1850s opened the African interior to European armies and traders.

nodes.label: Java cinchona plantations
nodes.desc: Seeds taken from the Andes despite export bans grew into Dutch plantations of high-yield Cinchona ledgeriana that dominated world quinine; a 1913 Quinine Agreement is called the first pharmaceutical cartel (checked, secondary). Japan's capture of Java in 1942 cut the Allies off.

nodes.label: Mosquito control
nodes.desc: Draining, oiling and screening against mosquitoes once their role was known. The French Panama canal lost perhaps 20,000 workers to fever (rough); the American canal succeeded after Gorgas's campaign (1904 to 1914).

nodes.label: Hookworm eradication
nodes.desc: The Rockefeller Sanitary Commission's campaign (1909 to 1914) raised school attendance and later earnings in the most infected counties (Bleakley 2007, unchecked): disease as a tax on human capital.

nodes.label: Rinderpest in Africa
nodes.place: Horn of Africa to the Cape, 1887 to 1897
nodes.desc: Cattle plague swept from the Horn to the Cape and killed perhaps 80 to 90% of cattle in many places (rough), bringing famine to herders and bush and tsetse onto abandoned grazing. Rinderpest was declared eradicated in 2011 (memory).

nodes.label: Compulsory cull with compensation
nodes.desc: Britain's cattle plague of 1865 to 1867 brought compulsory slaughter with compensation and a state veterinary service (memory): the state destroying private beasts to protect a shared stock, repeated in the 2001 foot-and-mouth cull (about six million animals, rough).

nodes.label: Household herbal healing
nodes.desc: Most healing in history was done at home, mostly by women, with simples from the garden and hedge; cunning folk and wise women sold it by reputation. It needs plant knowledge passed down, and no institution.

nodes.label: Licensed midwives
nodes.desc: Midwifery was licensed by English bishops from the early 16th century (memory), with oaths not to hide or swap infants; men-midwives with forceps entered in the 18th century, and the Midwives Act came in 1902 (memory).

nodes.label: Barber-surgeons
nodes.desc: A craft of the hands (bleeding, bones, teeth, wounds, amputations), organised as a guild with apprentices; London's Company of Barber-Surgeons dates from 1540 (memory). Armies were its school.

nodes.label: Licensed physicians
nodes.place: Universities of Salerno, Montpellier, Paris; London
nodes.desc: Learned diagnosis and prescription sold by university graduates, with a college licensing practice in a city (London 1518, memory). It held a monopoly that the apothecaries later broke.

nodes.label: Apothecaries' Society
nodes.desc: Apothecaries left the Grocers' Company for their own Society in 1617; the Rose case (Lords, 1704) let them prescribe as well as dispense, and the 1815 Act made the Society the licensing body for general practice (all checked). The general practitioner grew from the drug shop.

nodes.label: Drug and spice trade
nodes.place: Venice, Alexandria, Canton; caravan and monsoon routes
nodes.desc: An apothecary's shelves drew on world trade: pepper and ginger, Chinese rhubarb, Socotra aloes, Egyptian senna, opium, sugar as medicine, guaiacum wood for syphilis (a Fugger monopoly, memory) and Venetian theriac certified by officials. High value for weight, few ports of entry, adulteration a constant risk.

nodes.label: Bimaristan hospitals
nodes.desc: Endowed hospitals of the Islamic world with wards, physicians and pharmacies, paid for by waqf; Cairo's al-Mansuri dates from 1284 (memory). They join charity, endowment and learned medicine.

nodes.label: Charitable hospitals
nodes.desc: Monastic infirmaries and endowed hospitals gave beds, food and care; 18th-century voluntary hospitals ran on subscriptions and became teaching and surgical centres (memory). Later the rates and the state paid.

nodes.label: Patent medicines
nodes.desc: Branded remedies sold by advertisement, among the largest advertisers in 18th- and 19th-century newspapers; a market in hope before drug acts and proof of efficacy.

nodes.label: Bengal opium monopoly
nodes.desc: The East India Company held a monopoly of Bengal opium and sold it to private traders who smuggled it into China to pay for tea; silver began to flow out of China, and the Opium Wars (1839 to 1842, 1856 to 1860) followed (memory). Drug, luxury, smuggling and finance in one chain.

nodes.label: Smallpox inoculation and vaccine
nodes.desc: Inoculation with smallpox matter came to England from the Ottoman world in 1721; Jenner's cowpox vaccine (1796) was the first mass preventive, made from cows (memory). It began the end of the crowd diseases' toll.

nodes.label: Mortality statistics
nodes.place: London bills of mortality; Farr's registration
nodes.desc: Weekly bills of mortality and then civil registration (1837) with William Farr's analysis showed which districts killed (memory). Statistics made the case for sanitation and public health.

nodes.label: Urban penalty
nodes.desc: Industrial crowding made towns deadlier before they became healthier: life expectancy in Manchester and Liverpool in the 1830s and 1840s ran well below England's average (Szreter, unchecked). Typhoid, tuberculosis and infant diarrhoea killed more than cholera, but cholera moved Parliament.

nodes.label: Local wood famines
nodes.desc: Woods near towns and fuel-hungry trades were cut faster than they grew, so fuel and great timber became dear within carting range. Nef's national 'timber crisis' is contested: ironmasters managed coppices and the shortage was local (Flinn, Hammersley). The answers were moving industry, managing woods, laws, or coal.

nodes.label: Smoke nuisance rules
nodes.desc: A royal proclamation of 1306 against burning sea coal in London (memory) and Evelyn's Fumifugium (1661) proposals to move smoky trades out had little effect for three centuries.

nodes.label: Tokugawa regenerative forestry
nodes.desc: Old-growth forest was logged out by about 1670 for castles, temples and towns; felling bans and inventories, then planted forests, turned exploitation to regeneration (Totman 1989, checked as an argument), partly by coercion and partly by village self-rule over common woods.

nodes.label: Chesapeake tobacco and old fields
nodes.desc: Tobacco drew hard on the soil: planters cropped a field three or four years, left it as old field and cleared new ground (rough). The economy moved west with the frontier and leaned on enslaved labour to clear land; marl and lime came later as remedies (memory).

nodes.label: Dust Bowl and soil conservation
nodes.desc: Ploughing the Plains in wet years, then drought and wind, blew the soil away in the 1930s; the Soil Conservation Service (1935), contour ploughing, shelterbelts and paying farmers to retire land answered it (memory).

nodes.label: Aral Sea and modern salinity
nodes.place: Amu Darya and Syr Darya basins; the Indus
nodes.desc: Soviet cotton irrigation took the rivers that fed the Aral Sea, which shrank to a small fraction of its volume with salt and dust blown off its bed (memory). Canal irrigation in the Indus basin waterlogged and salted land until tube wells lowered the water (rough).

nodes.label: Megafauna extinctions
nodes.desc: Mammoths, giant sloths and other large animals vanished as people arrived; human overkill against climate change is contested. The first depletion of a wild stock.

nodes.label: Bison hide hunt
nodes.desc: Once tanners could use bison hides for belting and leather and railways could carry them, hunters cut perhaps 30 to 60 million bison (c. 1800) to about 500 to 540 counted by Hornaday in 1889 (checked). A commons taken for a distant market.

nodes.label: Wildlife trade law
nodes.desc: The Lacey Act (1900) banned interstate trade in game taken illegally (memory): regulating the market rather than the hunt.

nodes.label: Whaling convention and moratorium
nodes.desc: Right, bowhead, sperm and blue whales were hunted down in turn; the 1946 convention and the 1986 moratorium closed the hunt (memory).

nodes.label: Close seasons and net rules
nodes.desc: Medieval rivers had close seasons for salmon, rules on net mesh and on weirs that blocked the whole river, and fisheries let by lease (memory; Magna Carta's weir clause in part 05).

nodes.label: River pollution law
nodes.desc: The Rivers Pollution Prevention Act 1876 (memory) followed the Great Stink and the sewers: the river as a shared sink brought under statute.

nodes.label: Clean Air Act
nodes.desc: London's smog of December 1952 killed about 4,000 by the count at the time and 10,000 to 12,000 by later estimates (checked); the Clean Air Act 1956 brought smokeless zones and controls on domestic and industrial smoke (checked).

nodes.label: Leaded petrol
nodes.desc: Tetraethyl lead stopped engine knock and spread lead into the air and children's blood worldwide; phased out by 2021 (memory). A pollution built into a fuel.

nodes.label: Sulphur cap-and-trade
nodes.desc: Tradable allowances for power stations' sulphur dioxide cut acid rain at lower cost than expected (rough): pricing a sink.

nodes.label: Montreal Protocol
nodes.desc: The 1987 treaty phased out CFCs that thinned the ozone layer (memory): the clearest global commons regulated successfully.

nodes.label: Carbon pricing
nodes.desc: Permits or taxes on carbon dioxide, with standards and subsidies for substitutes; the atmosphere as a priced commons (memory).

nodes.label: Greenland walrus ivory
nodes.place: Norse Greenland to Norway and Europe
nodes.desc: Norse Greenland paid its way in walrus ivory; when elephant ivory returned to Europe and the climate cooled, the colony lost its export and was abandoned in the 15th century (contested). A trade-dependent outpost rather than a simple ecocide.

nodes.label: Pepper and spice trade
nodes.place: Malabar coast; Red Sea; Venice and Alexandria
nodes.desc: Pepper from Malabar, cinnamon from Ceylon, cloves and nutmeg from the Moluccas and Banda: high value for weight paid for monsoon voyages and caravans. Venice and Alexandria held the western end until the Portuguese Cape route (1498).

nodes.label: Banda nutmeg monopoly
nodes.desc: Nutmeg and mace grew only on the Bandas. The Dutch East India Company took them in 1621, killing, enslaving or driving out most of perhaps 13,000 to 15,000 people (checked as to the range), and replanted them as slave-worked groves.

nodes.label: Byzantine silk monopoly
nodes.desc: Silkworm eggs smuggled from Central Asia in the 550s (Procopius, memory) let Byzantium make silk under imperial workshops and a state monopoly; Lucca, Venice and Lyon followed.

nodes.label: Tyrian purple
nodes.desc: Dye from murex snail glands: about 12,000 snails gave 1.4 g in Friedländer's 1908 to 1909 experiment (checked), enough to trim one garment. Purple marked Roman senators and Byzantine emperors, and imperial workshops held its monopoly.

nodes.label: Cochineal
nodes.desc: Scale insects raised on prickly pear by Indigenous households; about 70,000 dried insects to a pound of red dye, and New Spain's second export after silver (checked, secondary). Spain kept the insect at home; aniline dyes ended its reign after 1856.

nodes.label: Canton tea trade
nodes.desc: Chinese tea bought at Canton through licensed merchants under the East India Company's monopoly became Britain's mass drink; high duties made it the most smuggled good until 1784, and opium paid for it later.

nodes.label: Tea transferred to India
nodes.desc: Robert Fortune took tea plants and growers out of China in 1848 to 1851 (memory); Assam and Ceylon plantations ended China's monopoly.

nodes.label: Meissen porcelain
nodes.desc: Böttger and Tschirnhaus made European hard-paste porcelain about 1708 to 1710 (memory), under the Saxon elector's monopoly and secrecy, ending dependence on Chinese imports.

nodes.label: Wedgwood creamware
nodes.desc: Josiah Wedgwood sold 'Queen's Ware' to the middle classes with royal patronage, showrooms, pattern books, travellers and fixed prices: the consumer revolution as marketing (McKendrick).

nodes.label: Sumptuary laws
nodes.place: Rome, Italian cities, England, Ming China, Tokugawa Japan
nodes.desc: Laws fixing who might wear, eat or display what. England's Statute concerning Diet and Apparel of 1363 (checked) answered post-plague wages; others aimed to stop bullion leaving or protect home industry. Widely evaded; status goods are positional.

nodes.label: Great-household hospitality
nodes.desc: Lords spent much of their income on food, drink, livery cloth and hospitality (Dyer: often half or more on food and drink, rough): surplus turned into standing, retainers and alliance.

nodes.label: Consumer revolution
nodes.desc: Households bought far more china, pewter, clocks, looking-glasses, printed cottons and tea things from the later 17th century (Weatherill, Shammas; counts unchecked). With the industrious revolution, demand that pulled proto-industry and the factory.

nodes.label: Fashion as an industry
nodes.place: Lyon silk; Paris fashion dolls and plates
nodes.desc: Lyon's designers changed silk patterns each season and fashion dolls and plates carried styles across Europe (memory); Simmel's trickle-down: the rich move on as others imitate.

nodes.label: Luxury brand groups
nodes.desc: Personal luxury goods are a market of a few hundred billion euros a year (about 360 billion in 2023, rough), with margins from brands, controlled scarcity and owned retail rather than materials.

nodes.label: De Beers diamond cartel
nodes.desc: De Beers controlled most rough diamond trade for much of the 20th century and marketed scarcity ('a diamond is forever', 1947), until supply diversified and synthetics arrived (memory).

nodes.label: Counterfeit goods
nodes.desc: Fake brands and medicines put at about 2.5% of world trade in 2016 (OECD and EUIPO, rough): luxury's and pharma's shadow trade.

nodes.label: Hue and cry
nodes.desc: Anyone robbed raised the cry and all had to follow the thief from village to village (memory): policing as a duty of neighbours, beside frankpledge.

nodes.label: Watch and ward
nodes.desc: The Statute of Winchester (1285) shut town gates at night, set watchmen and cleared brush 200 feet each side of highways against ambush (memory).

nodes.label: Thief-takers
nodes.desc: Private recovery of stolen goods for reward; Jonathan Wild (hanged 1725) ran theft and return together (memory). Recovery by reward before prevention by patrol.

nodes.label: Bow Street Runners
nodes.desc: Paid officers attached to a magistrate (1749, memory): the step between thief-takers and the Metropolitan Police.

nodes.label: Brigandage and highway robbery
nodes.place: Roads of Eurasia; later Europe, the Balkans, China
nodes.desc: Bandits thrived where states were weak or borders near; Hobsbawm's social bandit is contested by Blok. Caravans went armed or escorted, and states that cleared the roads widened markets.

nodes.label: Cilician piracy
nodes.desc: Raids and slaving that fed Delos's slave market until Pompey's command of 67 BCE cleared the sea (memory).

nodes.label: Wokou piracy
nodes.desc: Japanese and Chinese smugglers and raiders fed by Ming bans on private sea trade; the raids fell after the ban was lifted in 1567 (memory). Piracy as the shadow of a trade ban.

nodes.label: Barbary corsairs
nodes.desc: Raids on ships and coasts for ransom and slaves: Davis estimates 1 to 1.25 million Europeans enslaved 1530 to 1780 (checked as his estimate; contested). States paid tribute or sent fleets.

nodes.label: Privateering
nodes.desc: States licensed private ships to seize enemy merchants: war as a business, ended among signatories by the Declaration of Paris (1856, memory).

nodes.label: Somali piracy
nodes.place: Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean
nodes.desc: Ransom piracy cost $7 to 12 billion in 2010 and about $7 billion in 2011, of which ransoms were about 2%; faster steaming, patrols, guards and insurance were the rest (Oceans Beyond Piracy, checked). The cost of predation is mostly the cost of avoiding it.

nodes.label: Tea smuggling
nodes.desc: With duties near 119%, gangs such as the Hawkhurst Gang ran much of England's tea in from the Continent; the Commutation Act of 1784 cut the duty to 12.5% and legal sales rose (checked).

nodes.label: Commutation Act duty cut
nodes.desc: The tea duty cut from 119% to 12.5% (checked) took the smugglers' margin: a lower duty raising more revenue, as Adam Smith argued.

nodes.label: Gabelle and salt smuggling
nodes.desc: France's salt tax made salt many times dearer in some provinces than others; the faux-sauniers who carried it across were hunted by a large armed customs force (memory).

nodes.label: Milled coin and recoinage
nodes.desc: Hammered coin invited clipping and sweating; milled edges from 1662 and the Great Recoinage of 1696 under Newton at the Mint answered it (memory).

nodes.label: Hallmarking
nodes.desc: The goldsmiths' assay and mark guaranteed silver and gold fineness from 1300 (memory): a guild search turned into a standard.

nodes.label: Cloth seals and searchers
nodes.desc: Royal aulnagers and guild searchers measured and sealed each cloth against stretching and short length (memory): a seal as a quality and measure certificate.

nodes.label: Food adulteration
nodes.desc: Alum in bread, water in milk and beer, coloured tea leaves; Accum's treatise (early 19th century) exposed it. Cheating grew with the distance between maker and buyer.

nodes.label: Food and drug purity acts
nodes.desc: The Bradford sweets poisoning of 1858 (over 200 poisoned, 21 dead, checked) helped pass the Adulteration of Food Act (1860), then the Sale of Food and Drugs Act (1875, memory), with public analysts.

nodes.label: Guard labour
nodes.desc: Police, guards, supervisors and prison staff as a share of the workforce, larger where inequality is higher (Bowles and Jayadev, contested): labour taken from making to protect what is made.

nodes.label: Equal-arm balance
nodes.desc: The balance and set weights let silver, metals and spices be traded and taxed by weight; with sworn weights it is the first measuring instrument of trade.

nodes.label: Qin standardisation
nodes.desc: In 221 BCE the Qin made weights, measures, coin, script and axle widths one across the empire, with inscribed standard weights (memory).

nodes.label: Exchequer standards
nodes.desc: Magna Carta clause 35 (1215) ordered one measure of wine, ale and corn (the London quarter) and one breadth of dyed cloth through the realm (checked); standards kept at the Exchequer and copies sent to towns. Local measures survived for centuries.

nodes.label: Inspectors of weights and measures
nodes.desc: Local inspectors under 19th-century acts, later trading standards officers (memory), with imperial units made uniform in 1824.

nodes.label: Metric system
nodes.desc: Designed 1790 to 1795 from the meridian and water, decimal throughout; platinum metre and kilogram deposited 1799 and compulsory in France only from 1840 (memory). France had had hundreds of units in many local variants (unchecked).

nodes.label: Metre Convention and BIPM
nodes.desc: Signed on 20 May 1875 by seventeen states, it set up the International Bureau of Weights and Measures with new prototypes (checked); Britain signed in 1884 (checked).

nodes.label: SI from constants
nodes.desc: In 2019 every SI base unit was redefined from fixed constants of nature, the kilogram from Planck's constant (memory): the standard handed from a metal cylinder to physics.

nodes.label: Standard railway gauge
nodes.desc: The Gauge Act of 1846 after the 'gauge war' (memory) let wagons run through between companies.

nodes.label: Standard time zones
nodes.desc: Railway time from 1847, North American zones in 1883 and the Greenwich meridian in 1884 (memory) let timetables and telegraphs agree.

nodes.label: National standards laboratories
nodes.desc: State laboratories keeping and testing standards for industry (memory): measurement as a public good supplied by the state.

nodes.label: ISO
nodes.desc: The International Organization for Standardization (1947, memory) coordinates interface standards, among them container sizes.

nodes.label: Benchmark and test fraud
nodes.desc: The rigging of LIBOR (2012) and Volkswagen's emissions defeat device (2015): short weight in a measure that prices trillions or certifies millions of cars.
